sop_steps.detail: Check diagnostics first; a disapproval rate of about 0.3% is usually a sync issue, so resync, then sort products into top sellers, wasters, high-click/low-CVR and high-impression/low-CTR, leaving top sellers for last [Ecom Chris — d9kULGtUBD4 @ 00:02:53]

sop_steps.title: Rewrite titles for the top SKUs via supplemental feed
sop_steps.action: Sort by conversions, batch the top 30-50 SKUs, and push new titles through a supplemental feed.
sop_steps.detail: Use Brand + model + type or type + attribute + use case + brand, with no caps, symbols or promo text, and batch the top 30-50 SKUs sorted by conversions through a supplemental feed [Abdul Rauf Ali — V0LAr3jchLs @ 00:04:26]

sop_steps.title: Build custom labels with attribute rules
sop_steps.action: Create a rule on an unused custom label, preview, save as draft, apply, and segment in Google Ads.
sop_steps.detail: Data sources > Content API > Attribute rules > Add rule on custom_label_3; if title contains Christmas OR Santa OR holiday set 'Christmas', check the draft value in preview, apply, and it goes live on the next fetch [Grow My Ads — -w0GraOv2B0 @ 00:03:09]

sop_steps.title: Launch a test promotion and lock the review cadence
sop_steps.action: Run a 10-20% test promo with an 11:59 p.m. end time, then review diagnostics weekly and store quality monthly.
sop_steps.detail: Set up via Settings > Add-ons > Promotions with the code already live in the store and the end time at 11:59 p.m. [KeyCommerce — jmjy6G9akyM @ 00:01:32]; run a 10-20% test promo, check diagnostics weekly and store quality monthly [Max Crakanthorp — FZOo2bNTrzo @ 00:22:03]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over what leads the title. Austin at Grow My Ads puts household-name brands such as Nike, Apple and Samsung at the front and pushes unknown brands to the end. He argues the first 30 to 70 characters carry the weight, and Google may reorder words already in the title but never adds any [hY8ZBC3A4uQ @ 00:06:04]. His Home Reserve retitle to 'kid and pet friendly sectional sofa... washable' is the proof he points to for the benefit-led formula: a 10x jump in clicks and impressions, with sales rising. Kai Cromwell goes keyword-first, putting a phrase like 'leather office chair' ahead of the brand because only about 70 of the 150 characters are visible [W6w0BjjlBs4 @ 00:03:26]. Ecom Chris lands in the middle. He puts the brand first only when it is strong like Nike, and otherwise frontloads the main keyword. He also stacks attributes through the feed rather than hardcoding them, and never stacks synonyms [d9kULGtUBD4 @ 00:21:41]. Abdul Rauf Ali runs two templates depending on the catalog: brand plus model plus type, or type plus attribute plus use case plus brand. He sorts by conversions and only rewrites that slice first [V0LAr3jchLs @ 00:02:25]. The operator call: pick the template that matches your brand equity, then fill the visible zone with real search-term language.

Description depth splits the room just as hard. Max Crakanthorp treats the description as copy written 'for Google' and filled roughly 4,700 of 5,000 characters in his live build. He drafts with an AI prompt and then strips out irrelevant keywords [H4yH9xs030Q @ 00:06:23]. Ecom Chris says the description matters less than the title. He wants 200 to 500 characters, written for humans and leading with value, and warns that AI slop risks disapproval or higher CPC [XQTEnn-3t0E @ 00:07:28]. Austin at Grow My Ads applies an 80/20 rule: fix titles first and only write descriptions for top products [hY8ZBC3A4uQ @ 00:22:25]. The same fault line runs through image generation. Austin got a usable lifestyle scene from a single Nano Banana Pro prompt and uses Product Studio for background removal, upscaling and scene generation. KeyCommerce, by contrast, reports that Google's own generative image tool 'hasn't been that useful' [S1NhYxaPnic @ 00:05:00]. Both camps hold the same red line. Austin calls altering the product's look 'unethical', and he keeps the white-background main image while adding lifestyle shots as additional images. Testing method differs too: Max split-tests lifestyle versus plain images, either month versus month or across products.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The fastest way to lose a feed is a mismatch between what Merchant Center says and what the store shows. Max Crakanthorp always adds a sale price because the green sale price boosts clicks. But a sale price that does not match the website gets the product suspended [H4yH9xs030Q @ 00:13:46]. KeyCommerce's Sam says price and availability must be changed at the source, such as Shopify, because Google checks daily and a discrepancy brings quick disapproval [UcU7Ishu1lY @ 00:04:19]. Austin at Grow My Ads names the aggressive versions of the same play as suspension triggers: price baiting, checkout hacks and fake sale prices [hY8ZBC3A4uQ @ 00:03:19]. His alternative to faking a discount is honest price positioning, because in his words price will rule all, and a competitor 20% cheaper beats the best feed. Wixpa adds the trap that catches new Shopify stores: a perfect product feed does not guarantee product approval. Contact, refund, shipping, privacy and terms pages are still required, along with visible business details, and suspensions remain possible even after a clean app setup [RHJvGN_6sf0 @ 00:04:47]. The rule across all four is simple. Edit prices only where the store gets them, mirror them exactly, and treat every sale price as a live claim that Google checks daily.

History destruction is the quiet killer. KeyCommerce warns never to change an ID or SKU, because doing so would create a new product for Google. They report performance dropping after IDs were changed [S1NhYxaPnic @ 00:06:21]. The same video flags a second trap. If a feed app such as Semrush or DataFeedWatch runs the catalog, manual Merchant Center edits get overridden on the next sync, so all work belongs in the app. Wixpa calls the product ID format the migration trap. A new account keeps the default format, but a store switching apps must keep its previous format or lose its history [RHJvGN_6sf0 @ 00:02:18]. Wixpa also notes that inventory sync runs automatically once the app is connected and that a 'Pending' status is normal. Sync failures also masquerade as feed problems. Ecom Chris checks diagnostics first and reads a disapproval rate around 0.3% as usually a sync issue, fixed by a resync rather than a rewrite [d9kULGtUBD4 @ 00:02:53]. Max Crakanthorp hit the shipping version of the same bottleneck. He tells operators to turn off the Shopify shipping sync when disapprovals occur, then work through issues sorted by click potential, checking diagnostics weekly and store quality monthly [FZOo2bNTrzo @ 00:11:04].

The economics checks come down to data volume and waste. Ecom Chris tests one change per SKU and runs it for one to two weeks. He says that at $40 to $50 a day there is not enough data, because you need a lot of budget and a lot of data to test properly. His read on results: CTR rising while CVR falls means the title went too broad [d9kULGtUBD4 @ 00:30:17]. In the companion video he prices the downside of skipping the work. Poorly optimized feeds pay CPC two to three times higher, which he tracks alongside CTR, bounce rate, CVR and ROAS [XQTEnn-3t0E @ 00:23:16]. Abdul Rauf Ali runs a hygiene filter over six to twelve months: ROAS above 1.9, his breakeven, with at least 50 clicks. He gives the top performers a custom label [V0LAr3jchLs @ 00:08:40]. Tim Sutton's PMax client goes further on the cut side, excluding products with 100+ clicks and low ROAS [APb0cOGKROE @ 00:05:22]. Ecom Chris also warns of 'death by overoptimization', applying 80/20 with supplemental feeds for overrides. The operator takeaway for small budgets: batch only proven winners, cut proven losers on a click threshold, and resist rewriting the whole catalog at once.

callout.body: Each check maps to a suspension, a loss of product history, or wasted spend that practitioners hit firsthand.
items: Audit every sale price against the live site before it syncs, because a mismatch with the website gets the product suspended [Max Crakanthorp — H4yH9xs030Q @ 00:13:46].
Lock product IDs before any cleanup or app migration, because a changed ID creates a new product for Google and performance drops [KeyCommerce — S1NhYxaPnic @ 00:06:21].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I raise conversion rates and scale an e-commerce brand profitably from $0 to eight figures?
chapters.title: Conversion and Scaling to Eight Figures
chapters.subtitle: Shopify CRO to 4x conversion, stage-by-stage scaling from $0 to $10M+, cash-first and bootstrapped scaling (Bottle Keeper, Prestige Labs), when not to scale, financial metrics beyond ROAS, scaling ads on unit economics, the three scaling systems, operations-led growth, and omnichannel personalization and DTC in Europe
chapters.executive_summary: Operators agree that conversion and scaling are one math problem: revenue per visitor, contribution profit, and CAC payback decide whether more traffic makes money or just more noise. Davie Fogarty puts average Shopify stores at 1 to 3% conversion with the top 1% at 6 to 8%; Chase Chappell pegs the average at 1.4% and charges 7% of conversion for every second of load delay. Adam Callinan builds scale on pricing, AOV, conversion, a negative-log ad-budget curve, and MER over pixel attribution, while Leading Social and Bloom Analytics gate spend on 30 to 60 day payback. Splits are sharp: Justin Lalonde and Hormozi push hero SKUs and brand over SKU sprawl, Paul Waddy argues breadth across categories, and Lalonde insists many owners near $1M want better, not more.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The operators who have pushed brands past seven figures start from the same place: conversion rate is a lever on profit, not a trophy. Davie Fogarty frames the core math as revenue per visitor equals conversion rate times AOV, and calls profit per visitor the metric that really matters; anything that fails to lift RPV or PPV is noise, and a 5% conversion rate can leave a store worse off if it drags down AOV or raises costs [A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:01:42]. Chase Chappell runs the same arithmetic from the ad side: $10K of spend returning $30K at a 1% conversion rate becomes $60K to $90K at 2 to 3%, so ROAS climbs without touching the media budget [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:01:04]. Leading Social compresses it into one line, 'You don't scale revenue, you actually scale your contribution margin,' and calls revenue vanity while contribution margin is the oxygen of the business [KpmUvCBEKK4 @ 00:00:41]. Adam Callinan makes contribution profit the scoreboard: revenue minus every variable cost including ads, then minus fixed costs. In Callinan's worked example, $5k minus $3k leaves $2k of contribution profit, which turns into $500 of profit against $1.5k fixed or an $800 loss against $2.8k fixed [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:11:37].

The second point of agreement is that the offer and the price move conversion economics harder than button colors ever will. Fogarty mocks brands that split-test button colors 'like it's 2019' and defines the offer as price, bundles, upsells, guarantee and positioning, warning that copying competitors is the worst thing you can do [A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:05:08]. Callinan treats pricing as the first of five profit levers: with $200k of fixed costs and a 90% variable margin, breakeven sits at $2M, and a 10% price increase drops variable margin to 82%, lifts contribution margin from 10% to 18%, cuts breakeven to $1.38M and adds $250k at $2M of revenue [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:15:15]. Chappell tells brands under $100K a month to chase AOV before LTV and reports a bundle tool lifting AOV from $30 to $40 through $100-plus [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:19:03]. Trust is the shared prerequisite underneath the offer. Fogarty puts policies such as 'free returns within 30 days' and 'ships within 3 to 5 business days' directly under the add-to-cart button, and warns that buyers judge trust in 0.05 seconds, so ad, site and Instagram highlights must all match the brand [A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:11:42].

The third shared conviction is that paid traffic amplifies an offer that already works; it does not rescue one that does not. Justin Lalonde split with his own client on this point, insisting that paid marketing 'will not create demand' and only enhances existing demand, so core products have to be found before ads run [la7VuqSuHHE @ 00:02:32]. Paul Waddy applies the 80/20 rule to catalogs: 20% of products drive 80% of revenue, so an operator should expect 80% of launches to fail and keep testing rather than defend favorites [7v_KO8bj_G0 @ 00:13:07]. Nick Theriot's stage map opens the same way, with the $0 to $30k band devoted purely to offer validation: perceived value, target person and packaging, run on $50 to $100 a day, one campaign, five to six new ads a week, one product and one country [iacAWRoEwXI @ 00:00:00]. Once the offer converts, the gate to more spend is payback, not platform ROAS. Bloom Analytics reduces it to a rule of thumb, 'Pays back inside 60 days, you can spend more,' while warning that CAC climbs as gross profit holds flat, which quietly stretches the payback window [IlWyYcfaKpg @ 00:02:31].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Chase Chappell's diagnostic starts with speed, then reads the Shopify funnel stage by stage. Every one-second delay costs 7% of conversion, high-resolution images are the biggest drag, and the fix is the Tiny Image Optimizer app [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:01:49]. Next comes the add-to-cart ratio: a 2 to 5% ratio signals friction, missing information or sizing, a price set too high, or buttons buyers cannot see. A high add-to-cart rate with weak reached-checkout points to a cart page instead of a drawer cart, missing payment badges, shipping costs or broken discounts, and a low completed-checkout rate points to shipping thresholds, pricing, payment methods, trust badges or ship time [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:04:07]. Davie Fogarty calls the separate cart page 'the biggest mistake,' prescribes a slide-out drawer cart, and stacks PayPal, Apple Pay and Afterpay at checkout, with Shopify Markets auto-switching currency and language because, in Fogarty's words, 'I want an Australian seller in Australian dollars' [A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:15:54]. One Chappell teardown shows a pop-up, then a view-cart click, then a full cart page, plus a confusing 97-cent package-protection fee, and the verdict is blunt: 'This destroys conversion rates' [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:07:24].

On the offer, the numbers are specific. Fogarty's price test runs 5,000 visitors at $50 and 2% for 100 orders; at $55 the same conversion rate lifts revenue 10%, and even at 1.8% the $55 price lands $4,950 against $5,000 yet produces more profit through less customer service, less ops and a better COGS percentage, and Fogarty reports a price raise that actually pushed conversion up [A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:06:24]. Adam Callinan took Bottle Keeper from $20 to $40 over two years by adding a 10-cent tether, an opener lid and powder coating, and argues a move from $20 to $25 likely survives a 25% conversion-rate drop; the only real way to know what the market accepts is to test it [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:17:28]. Callinan's AOV structure prices a 2-pack at $75 instead of $80 and sells the third unit in a 3-pack at $30, so the per-unit discount deepens only as quantity climbs [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:19:03]. Chappell then pushes value after the card is charged: the checkout button reads 'Continue' rather than 'check out,' steering buyers into post-purchase upsells [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:17:02]. Both operators treat the bundle ladder as a margin decision rather than a discount reflex, and both test it live.

Scaling spend is its own set of mechanics. Callinan models ad budgets on a negative-log curve: with $100k of fixed costs and a 50% variable margin, breakeven ROAS is 22 at $10k of spend, 6 at $50k and 4 at $100k [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:25:39]. For measurement Callinan drops platform pixels as the source of truth, citing iOS 14.5 blocking and roughly 80% iPhone traffic, treats platform numbers with the instruction 'Use it as a baseline,' and runs MER or global ROAS alongside DTC ROAS that includes Amazon [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:30:31]. Nick Theriot's ladder sets the cadence: at $60k a month, raise Facebook spend 20% a day, test 10 to 20 ads a week and hire a Google or email agency; at $100k to $200k, spend $30k-plus and ship '22-40' ads a week; at $500k to $1M a month, spend runs around $150k with CAC rising; and at $1M to $2M, separate fully localized Shopify Plus stores go up per country [iacAWRoEwXI @ 00:01:17]. Theriot's cohort math shows why rising CAC is survivable: a $35 first order against a $62 CAC still reaches $132 of LTV by month 12, with breakeven around month two [iacAWRoEwXI @ 00:03:29].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split at the eight-figure line is catalog shape. Justin Lalonde runs fashion clients down from roughly 20 SKUs to about 10 and then to a 3-5 product hero collection. From there, Lalonde grows by iterating prints, colors, materials and creator partnerships on those winners, and points to an eight-figure single-product hoodie brand built on variations rather than SKU count [la7VuqSuHHE @ 00:04:25]. Paul Waddy openly pushes back on the single-product-all-the-way camp. Waddy argues that growth comes from extending into new categories instead of stacking variants, and accepts 80/20 math where most launches fail and testing never stops [7v_KO8bj_G0 @ 00:33:40]. The MoreMozi advice to a $5M-a-year travel-gear founder lands in the middle: lock in 5-7 cornerstone SKUs, then surround them with profit-maximized accessories that lift order count and lifetime value [raqfsvgSW0o @ 00:03:42]. Niche width splits the same way. Lalonde tells brands to niche down and keep messaging congruent with skaters, streetwear and basketball buyers. Noah Haynes warns that over-niching caps total addressable market and stalls growth after one or two years, citing a compression-sock brand that moved from hikers to runners with the identical product and only a new angle [SjGeVqhkKPw @ 00:00:36]. Operators have to pick which ceiling they would rather hit first.

Practitioners also disagree on whether scaling is even the goal. Justin Lalonde reports that only about half of agency clients want to maximize volume. The rest lock a fixed budget and chase ROI through 0.1-style micro-adjustments, and the agency's own mistake was assuming every client wanted to scale [rBcV_0ROMHM @ 00:01:17]. Lalonde frames fast scaling as a dirty bulk that taps out audiences and fatigues creative earlier, and tells owners to play their own game and brief their agencies on it. Alex Hormozi takes the opposite posture for an unsaturated market: treat profit as an experimentation budget and burn around $200k on keyword tests to find six that can each scale to $100k a month [bufdu58UUfo @ 00:01:15]. Paul Waddy sits between them, calling a land grab that only breaks even legitimate when cash runway supports it [7v_KO8bj_G0 @ 00:54:30]. On demand creation, Lalonde rejected a client's belief that ads create demand, arguing that paid marketing only enhances demand that already exists, so core products must be found before ads run [la7VuqSuHHE @ 00:02:32]. Waddy agrees that demand cannot be controlled but flips the lever to supply: hyper-limited monthly drops, collaborations and one-off releases, because raising spend mostly pushes frequency from one to five on the same people.

Testing discipline and discounting produce the loudest conflicts in conversion work. Davie Fogarty says 99% of brands do no CRO and the rest split-test button colors. Fogarty insists on one variable at a time, tracked in a spreadsheet, yet also says flatly that not everything needs testing [A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:12:55]. Adam Callinan puts numbers on the threshold: single-variable tests at around 3,000 visitors, and multivariate testing only once traffic reaches roughly 30,000 [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:20:55]. Chase Chappell treats CRO as continuous experimentation and leans hard into incentive mechanics. Those include an AI SMS recovery bot that offers a 5% or 10% discount and a full-width mystery-discount pop-up running near 15% email opt-in against a 3-5% norm [daDsoHXE52A @ 00:23:00]. Callinan's discount math cuts the other way: 10% off pushes variable margin from 50% to 56% and breakeven ROAS from 2 to 2.3, while 30% off drives breakeven ROAS to 3.45 [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:36:17]. Price direction splits too. Fogarty claims a price raise lifted conversion rate outright, and Callinan took a product from $20 to $40 over two years. Chappell, by contrast, tells brands under $100K a month to chase AOV through bundles before LTV. Whichever incentive an operator runs, it must clear contribution profit, not headline conversion rate.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest firsthand failures come from trusting platform numbers. Adam Callinan describes a $500k loss over roughly 16 months driven by overlapping 30-day attribution windows. The damage was compounded when iOS 14.5 blocked pixels on a traffic base that was about 80% iPhone [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:28:33]. The fix Callinan adopted was MER, or global ROAS, plus a DTC ROAS that folds in Amazon, used as a baseline rather than a scoreboard. Callinan pairs that with a breakeven ROAS curve derived from fixed costs and variable margin, because ad budgets without a mathematical framework are simply gambling [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:23:59]. Leading Social reaches the same conclusion from the agency side. MER divides total revenue by total marketing, including agency and content costs, which removes the channel bias where Meta can look strong while the business overall is under pressure [KpmUvCBEKK4 @ 00:02:48]. Paul Waddy adds the hidden ceiling behind rising spend: more budget mostly raises frequency from one to five, showing the same ad to the same people without opening new demand [7v_KO8bj_G0 @ 00:26:38]. Callinan's working rule is to chart the contribution-profit trend line and judge strategy by whether it climbs, regardless of what any dashboard claims about individual campaigns that month.

Cash and cost structure kill brands that look healthy on revenue. Paul Waddy calls inventory probably the number one reason brands go insolvent. Waddy prescribes about three months of stock cover, replenishment at 30 days, and four inventory turns a year. Supplier terms such as no deposit and payment 30 days after arrival turn months two and three into accumulated cash [7v_KO8bj_G0 @ 00:34:39]. Adam Callinan's firsthand reversal came from fixed costs: in 2019 the business gave back all of the profit earned in 2018. That loss drove a rule of keeping fixed costs under 20% of revenue and chasing more contribution profit with fewer fixed expenses [VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:41:34]. Bloom Analytics shows how thin the margin for error is. An $82 new-customer AOV minus $50 of variable costs leaves $32 of gross unit profit, and a $50 CAC drives first-order contribution to minus $18. Repeat purchases only reach breakeven around day 56, a close call against the 60-day target [IlWyYcfaKpg @ 00:01:38]. The trap is that CAC keeps climbing while gross profit stays flat, so payback quietly stretches past the window that justified spending more [IlWyYcfaKpg @ 00:02:31]. Revenue growth alone hides every one of these leaks until the bank balance says otherwise.

Operational breakage and strategic drift form the third failure cluster. Justin Lalonde puts it bluntly: when you scale fast, operations and supply chain break, which is why owners near $1M often push for better rather than more [rBcV_0ROMHM @ 00:04:41]. Frankly eCommerce founders Emelin and Randy lived it, falling weeks behind during the 2023 holiday. They rebuilt in-house fulfillment around coded Kallax shelf locations, separate pickers and packers, and back-planned design deadlines, and orders now ship on time [CCtunt0iWMU @ 00:34:16]. Alex Hormozi diagnoses a slower trap in a $3M run-rate, four-SKU brand. Media arbitrage stops working around $10-12M, and the direct response doom loop ends at something like $12M with 7% margins. The fix is cutting losing SKUs and building a brand, because acquirers buy brands [bufdu58UUfo @ 00:13:29]. Hormozi also rejected a $500k SaaS build with $120k a year in upkeep for a salon and wholesale operator, calling the pull to keep investing sunk cost fallacy. In Hormozi's words, some of the best money you ever spend is deciding to stop spending bad money [bufdu58UUfo @ 00:21:43]. MoreMozi adds a creative trap at scale: Meta's Andromeda update requires truly net-new creatives, not recycled variations of old winners.

callout.title: Do Not Raise Spend Until These Four Checks Clear
callout.body: Each gate comes from a loss, stall or near-miss that a practitioner reported firsthand. Clear all four before pushing budget, adding a market, or committing to a new inventory buy [Adam Callinan — VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:23:59].
items: CAC payback sits inside 30-60 days; six months or more means you are financing growth and need working capital lined up first [Leading Social — KpmUvCBEKK4 @ 00:01:48].
Breakeven ROAS for the planned budget is calculated from fixed costs and variable margin, since it runs 22 at $10k spend, 6 at $50k and 4 at $100k [Adam Callinan — VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:25:39].
If revenue has been stuck near $80k a month for 3 months while MER rises, bring in an agency instead of forcing more self-run spend [Growth Manifesto Podcast — 7v_KO8bj_G0 @ 00:29:01].
Fulfillment can absorb the volume, with a separate picker and packer giving two points of verification before holiday or launch surges [Frankly eCommerce — CCtunt0iWMU @ 00:07:53].

chapters.pull_quote: "So ad budgets without any mathematical framework behind them feels like gambling because honestly it is just gambling." Adam Callinan (VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:23:59).
action_checklist: Build per-new-customer unit economics: new-customer AOV minus product, packaging, shipping, transaction and platform fees, minus CAC, net of returns and refunds [Bloom Analytics — IlWyYcfaKpg @ 00:00:47].

Diagnose the funnel stage by stage: a 2-5% add-to-cart rate signals friction or missing info, and a high ATC with low reached-checkout points to the cart page, badges, shipping costs or broken discounts [Chase Chappell — daDsoHXE52A @ 00:04:07].
Test price increases of 5%, 10% and 20%, knowing that a move from $20 to $25 likely survives a 25% conversion-rate drop [Adam Callinan — VCXWZQgbKXw @ 00:17:28].
Mine objections from Amazon, TikTok and Reddit and answer them in the PDP, ad copy and pinned comments [Davie Fogarty Mentors — A-7pTamjBIw @ 00:11:02].

Seed products to aesthetic-fit creators without expectations, move responsive creators to a retainer, pay-per-video or discount code, and run Spark Ads from their accounts [Justin Lalonde — la7VuqSuHHE @ 00:08:01].
Report MER as total revenue divided by total marketing, including agency and content costs, before trusting any single platform's ROAS [Leading Social — KpmUvCBEKK4 @ 00:02:48].
